title: Marguerite and the Portrait
premise: Folklorist Wren Voss arrives in the isolated village of Marguerite's Hollow to record its songs, only to find the villagers sing each one exactly once and refuse to repeat a note. Analyzing his overnight sleep recordings, Wren discovers a second voice—dry, patient, answering questions he never asked aloud—that claims the village's founders bound something beneath the church to buy their prosperity, and the binding is failing. The voice, Marguerite, was the founders' sacrificed partner, erased from every record and every memory, and she needs a living outsider to complete the counter-ritual and free her. As Wren uncovers that his own arrival was engineered—his grandmother was born in the Hollow and fled—he must choose between sealing Marguerite away again, as the villagers demand, or finishing the ritual, which will return the village's stolen memories to everyone at once, including the guilt of what they did. He completes it: Marguerite is released, the village remembers everything, and Wren, no longer invisible, leaves with recordings no one will ever sing twice.
about_author: Isandro Zhou is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal settlements before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folklore, believing the scariest stories are the ones communities agree never to repeat.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Its Doors
chapters.summary: Wren arrives in Marguerite's Hollow, renting a crooked house whose previous tenant left behind numbered door labels and a warning chalked inside a cupboard. The villagers are polite but watchful. When he asks about local songs, they sing beautifully—once—then change the subject. Wren's POV; establishes unease, his habit of counting and recording as a shield against belonging.

chapters.title: Songs Sung Once
chapters.summary: Wren begins fieldwork, coaxing a lullaby from the innkeeper's daughter, Maren, who sings it flawlessly then goes white when he asks for a second take. The village priest, Aldous Crane, gently insists some songs are 'spent.' Wren notices every house has a small unmarked door. His POV; the theme of enforced forgetting surfaces.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Reviewing his sleep recordings at 3 a.m., Wren hears a woman's voice answering questions he never asked—dry, amused, patient. She knows his name. He checks the recorder: it was running unplugged. Terrified but scholarly, he begins leaving questions on tape before bed. His POV; dread mixed with the thrill of discovery.

chapters.title: Marguerite
chapters.summary: The voice names herself Marguerite and tells him the founders were four, not three—the fourth was given to the church's foundations so the village would never hunger. Every record of her was burned; every memory of her was sung away. Wren finds her face scratched out of the founding portrait in the church. His POV; the horror of deliberate erasure.

chapters.title: The Portrait's Fourth Figure
chapters.summary: Wren photographs the founding portrait and, in the image, a fourth figure stands where the wall is blank to the eye. Maren sees the photo and flees; that night someone breaks in and steals his recorder, leaving a fresh count chalked on his door: the number is falling. His POV; he realizes the village is watching him back.

chapters.title: What the Village Gave Up
chapters.summary: In the church archive Wren finds the founders' ledger: harvests that never failed, winters that never killed—and a debt column that never zeroes. Marguerite explains the ritual must be renewed each generation, and the current binding is decades overdue. Crane confronts Wren, offering him a train ticket and silence. His POV; the corruption of inherited comfort laid bare.

chapters.title: The Debt Comes Due
chapters.summary: Things sour: crops gray overnight, Maren's little brother stops speaking, and the unmarked doors in every house begin bleeding at the seams. The villagers, desperate, decide Wren himself is the renewal payment—his grandmother fled the Hollow owing a debt. They come for him at night with lanterns and hymnals. His POV; belonging revealed as a trap.

chapters.title: Beneath the Church
chapters.summary: Wren escapes into the church's undercroft through the smallest unmarked door, guided by Marguerite's voice, and finds her: not a demon but a woman fused into the foundation stone, kept alive by the songs sung once, each one a nail. She shows him the counter-ritual's final verse—which only an outsider who has been given a true memory can sing. His POV; pity transforms fear.

chapters.title: The Verse No One Will Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Climax. Crane and the villagers corner Wren at the stone; Marguerite, to arm him, pours her one remaining memory into him—his grandmother as a child, watching her own mother help bind Marguerite, and choosing to flee rather than forget. Wren sings the final verse as the villagers' stolen memories return all at once, and they collapse under the weight of what they've inherited. His POV; the cost of remembering.

chapters.title: Everything Remembered
chapters.summary: The stone crumbles; Marguerite steps out old and mortal and free, and the village must live with its full history—grief, guilt, and the lullabies that can finally be sung twice. Crane, aged by truth, asks Wren to erase the recordings; Wren refuses, but leaves them with the village, unplayed. He boards the train with one tape of his own: a woman's voice, laughing, no longer answering questions. His POV; belonging earned by witness, not invisibility.
